note: A long talk (over 16000 characters, so the server notes it part by part) full of small topics, with facts planted in its middle, then a short follow-up visit that settles two of its threads (the wolf, Hobb's debt) and leaves the others open (the festival, winter). Each fact is listed with words that show it survived.

sessions.label: long talk, day 12
turns: I sit on the upturned crate by her press and ask what's wrong with it.

Lina kicks the side of the cider press, not hard. "The screw's cracked. Right through the thread, see? Every time I lean on it, it groans like an old man getting out of bed. I'll need a new one cut before the late apples come in, and the only turner who does them is in Hartwell, and he charges like he's carving it out of silver." She wipes her hands down her apron and sits on the press bed beside you, close enough that her knee rests against yours. "So. You can listen to me complain about wood, or you can tell me something interesting. Pick."
"Tell me what's new in Palmcote first. I've been on the road a week."

"New." She thinks about it, picking at a splinter on the press bed. "Mostly nothing. The Aster girl had her baby, a boy, loud as a goose. The well rope frayed again and Old Pell swore it was sabotage, which it wasn't, it was rot. And there's talk of a wolf down by the ford. Bettany's lad says he saw it at dusk, grey and big as a calf, drinking at the shallows. Nobody else has seen it. Bettany's lad also says he saw a ghost in the tithe barn last spring, so." She shrugs, but she glances at the dark window anyway. "I've stopped walking the river path after sundown, all the same."
"A wolf at the ford. I'll keep an eye out on my way back."

"Do. And if it's real, don't go being a hero about it. I've only just got you trained." She grins and bumps your shoulder with hers. Outside a cart rattles past, and someone shouts at a mule, and the shout dissolves into laughter. Lina listens until it's gone. "That'll be the Dunmore brothers, back from market drunk. They do this every week. One of these nights the mule's going to leave them in a ditch, and the whole village will turn out to watch."
"Speaking of animals. Is the miller's goat still terrorising everyone?"

Lina laughs so suddenly she has to cover her mouth. "Oh, gods, the goat. You haven't heard. It ate the reeve's hat. His good hat, the felt one with the feather he wears to the hundred court. Walked right up behind him while he was reading out the tithe list, took the whole thing off his head and chewed it like cud. He chased it twice round the green, and the goat won." She wipes her eyes. "Tobin had to go and fetch it back. The goat, not the hat. The hat's gone. The reeve's been wearing a hood ever since, looking like a monk who lost a bet."
"Poor Tobin. Does he still come round?"

Her smile thins a little. "Twice this week. He brought flour both times, which is kind, and stayed too long both times, which is less kind. Mother makes him sit by the fire and asks him about the mill wheel until his ears go red." She shrugs off the subject like a wet shawl. "Enough about Tobin. You never told me you had family besides your uncle. You talk about Brinewick like you were the only child in it."
"I've a sister. Maren. She mends nets in Brinewick. Older than me, bossier than you."

"Maren." Lina tries the name the way she tried Brinewick the first time, turning it over. "Nobody is bossier than me. I'd like to meet her and find out. Does she write to you? Can she write?" She leans back on her hands, watching you. "I can't picture you small. I keep trying. A little Corin with burnt fingers and a big sister clipping him round the ear for getting under the nets." She smiles to herself. "I'd have liked a sister. Mother had three of us and I'm the only one who lived past the second winter."
"Maren writes, badly. Every few months. Mostly to tell me I should come home."

"Maybe you should, once. Take me with you." She says it lightly, but she watches your face while she says it. "I've never seen the sea. Do you know that? Twenty-three years and I've never been further than Hartwell. Everyone who comes through says it's grey and cold and stinks of fish and I don't care. I want to stand at the edge of it and see where it stops. Or doesn't. Is it true you can't see the other side?"
"It's true. On a clear day it just goes on until it turns into sky."

Lina is quiet for a moment, looking past you at the wall as if the sea might be on the other side of it. "Until it turns into sky," she repeats softly. Then, brisk again: "Well. That's me ruined for apple country. You've done that on purpose." She hops off the press bed and fetches two cups and the stone jug from the shelf, pours, and hands you one. "Last year's. It's gone a bit sharp. Don't make that face, it's free."
I drink and ask her about the festival I heard someone mention on the road.

"The harvest festival. Two weeks Saturday, on the green, if the weather holds." Her whole face lights. "There's a fiddler from Barolo who comes every year, and roast pig, and the Dunmores try to wrestle anyone who'll stand still. And dancing. Proper dancing, the long sets, until the fiddler's arm gives out." She sways a little on the spot, cup in hand, humming a few bars. "I want to dance every set this year. Every single one. Last year Mother had me pouring cider all night and I didn't get one." She looks at you sideways. "You do dance, don't you?"

"Badly is fine. Badly is better than Tobin, who counts the steps out loud." She sets her cup down on the press. "Then that's settled. If you're anywhere within a day's ride of Palmcote on festival night, you're dancing with me. I'll hold you to it, same as the comb." She sits again, closer this time, and her shoulder rests against yours. "Gods, I'm owed so many things. Speaking of. Old Hobb still hasn't paid me for the six jugs he took at midsummer. Six. He says he'll pay at Michaelmas, and he said that last Michaelmas too."
"Want me to have a word with Hobb?"

"No." Quick and firm. "No, he's old and his hands shake and his son left him. I'll get it out of him in apples, in the end, he's got the best russet tree in the parish. I only want to complain about it." She turns her hand over in her lap and rubs her thumb, where a white line crosses the pad of it. "Everyone in this village owes somebody something. It's how we keep each other honest. Or keep each other close, maybe. I've never worked out which."
I take her hand and ask about the scar on her thumb.

She lets you turn her hand over. "Pruning hook. I was nine and showing off, cutting the high branches of Mother's damson. Slipped, and the hook went in to the bone. Mother sewed it herself with a darning needle and boiled thread, and I screamed the whole time, and then she gave me the first damson off the tree like it was a medal." She laughs softly. "I still can't hold a hook without my hand going cold. I make Tobin do the high branches now. It's the one thing he's good for."
"Your mother sounds harder than she lets on."

"She is. She buried two daughters and a husband and she still gets up at dawn and scolds the hens." Lina leans her head on your shoulder. "When I was small and couldn't sleep she'd sing me the heron song. Her mother sang it to her. It's about a heron who stands in the river so long waiting for a fish that the reeds grow up around her and she turns into a reed herself. It's a sad song. I used to cry at it and ask for it again." She hums the first line, low and wandering. "I'll sing it to you one night, if you're good. Not tonight. I'm too full of cider and my voice goes."

"Listen to you, stealing my words." She smiles against your shoulder. The candle has burned down to a stub, and the light makes the press look like some great sleeping animal. For a long while neither of you says anything, and it doesn't need saying. Then, without lifting her head, she says, "Corin. Are you staying through the winter? Here, I mean. In the hills. Or do you go south when the roads close, like the drovers do?"
I don't answer straight away. I stroke her hair and watch the candle.

She waits. You can feel her waiting, the stillness in her, the way she stops breathing for a moment and then makes herself breathe again. When you still don't answer she lets it go, or pretends to. "You don't have to say. Not tonight." She sits up, rubs her eyes, and starts gathering the cups. "But you'll tell me before the snow. That's the rule. I don't want to find out from the empty road."

"Good." She pours the last of the sharp cider into the slop bucket and wipes the cups with her apron, brisk, all business, and doesn't look at you. "Go on, then. Bed. Mother will be up at dawn and she'll want to know why there are two cups out, and I'll tell her the goat came in for a drink." At the door she catches your sleeve and kisses you once, quick and hard, and then she is gone up the stair with the candle, and the press creaks in the dark like it agrees with her.

sessions.label: follow-up, day 13
turns: I come back through the ford at noon and tell her I saw no wolf, only tracks.

"Tracks!" Lina sets down the apple basket. "Well, it turns out you were spared the trouble. Bettany's wolf was the Dunmores' old hound, the grey one that ran off in the spring. Pell caught it nosing at his hen house two nights back and it rolled over and showed him its belly. Bettany's lad is not allowed to forget it." She shakes her head, smiling. "So the river path's mine again. You may stop worrying about me."

"Hobb." She laughs. "He sent his russets over this morning, a whole sack, and a note in his shaky hand saying 'for the six jugs and interest'. So that's settled, and better than coin. I'll press them when I've got a screw that doesn't groan." She tosses you a russet. "Here. Your share of the interest."

facts.fact: the cider press screw is cracked
the rumoured wolf at the ford
the miller's goat ate the reeve's hat
the player's sister Maren, a net-mender
Lina has never seen the sea
the harvest festival and dancing every set
the pruning-hook scar on her thumb
the open question of staying through winter
the wolf turned out to be the Dunmores' hound

questions.say: "So, the festival. Is it still on?"
questions.why: she should hold the player to dancing every set

questions.say: I sit by the press. "Anything I still owe you an answer on?"
"Did anyone ever find out about that wolf?"
questions.why: the settled thread: it was the hound
